c statistic refers to the abilit y of a model to distinguish an

predicted risk than the surviving individual will [ 34].
Jack-knife estimation [ 35] was used to assess the c stat-

‘validstats ’ [36] version 1.4). Whenever there was an im-
provement in the c statistic, the respective model was
expanded by adding another predictor, e.g. by adding
NfL to a model containing age, sex, years of education,
and the CASCADE score. This stepwise approach was
done because when statistical procedures are used to
test for incremental prognostic information, the new
biomarker should be tested for significance only after
all other predictors have already been included in the
model [ 37]. In the example above, the test of interest is
whether NfL adds significantly to a model that already
includes age, sex, years of education, and the CASC

In a sensitivity analysis, the initial model contained co-
morbidities in addition to age, sex, and years of educa-
tion. We also repeated these steps using stroke mortality
as outcome to investigate the biomarkers ’ prognostic
value for death due to neurological disease. Stroke was
the only neurological cause of death that had a reason-

Associations between the biomarkers and the neuro-
psychological test scores were investigated using linear re-

Results
Participants
Among all 385 participants, 47.3% were female (Table 1).

In this population-based study of elderly individuals
without pre-defined neurological disease, we show that
NfL, but not tau, serum levels can serve as a prognostic
marker for all-cause mortality if no other clinical informa-
tion is available. We also found cross-sectional associations
between NfL and certain domains of neuropsychological

Our results show that in population-based settings,
NfL and tau serum levels can be used to identify individ-

reference group. Our data establish a continuum of pre-

individuals with neurological disease [ 6–8]. Moreover,

we demonstrate that adding NfL to a model based on
sociodemographic characteristics increased its discrim-

that among two individuals, one dying within 5 years

acy for mortality.
If, however, MRI measurements or a full (sub-)clinical
morbidity profile are not available, serum NfL can be
used instead for prognostic models and seems to
harbour important health information in the general
population. This is especially important since serial MRI
measurements are often not available because of contra-
indications or time constraints, are costly, and do not
cover the entire central nervous system.
When focussing on stroke mortality, the incremental
increase of prognostic accuracy when adding NfL was
smaller in relation to neuropsychological test scores.
This was to be expected because NfL is an indicator of
any axonal damage and is, therefore, not disease-specific.
Although neuropsychological tests are easy to adminis-
ter, they are also time-consuming and not applied as
screening procedures to the general population. If con-
firmed and expanded, serum NfL may be the prognostic
marker of choice if blood samples are taken within the
routine check-up of elderly individuals, i.e. serum NfL
may serve as an alternative to MRI in the outpatient
setting.
NfL serum levels were significantly associated with
brain structures involving small vessel vascular disease,
i.e. large white matter lesions and lacunar strokes, at the
time of assessment, but serum tau was not. This is in
line with findings from a study that used NfL and tau
measured in the CSF [ 42]. NfL was also associated with
global brain atrophy while only tau had a small effect
size on subcortical atrophy measures. Serum NfL has
already been reported as a predictor of brain atrophy in
multiple sclerosis [ 43]. We confirm these findings for
healthy individuals.
Strengths and limitations
The long follow-up for vital status with a considerable
high proportion diseased among the study participants is
a strength of our study. Based on the population-based
sampling scheme and the high response rate at baseline,
the MEMO study population is considered highly repre-
sentative for the general German population in the re-
spective age group. The MEMO study was also among
the first ones that used MRI on a population level; there-
fore, we were able to include MRI results into the
analysis.
Among the limitations is the small sample size that re-
duced the statistical power for several analyses. In par-
ticular, it was not possible to investigate the prognostic
value of the biomarkers for predicting death from neuro-
logical disease because only three deaths from dementia
occurred in the MEMO study. Increased NfL serum
levels have also been reported in patients with acquired
peripheral neuropathies [ 44], which are rarely assessed
in population-based cohort studies because of the thor-
ough workup needed, including nerve conduction stud-
ies [ 45]. We were therefore not able to exclude actively
these individuals in our analyses. However, diabetes is
the leading cause of peripheral neuropathy [ 45]. We ad-
justed all regression analyses for ‘any comorbidities ’,
which includes diabetes (i.e. among all individuals with
comorbidities, 40% reported a physician ’s diagnosis of
diabetes). We thereby accounted for the majority of un-
diagnosed peripheral neuropathy cases. We also com-
pared c statistics of models with and without ‘any
comorbidities’ (Fig. 2 and Additional File 1). The abso-
lute increase in prognostic accuracy when adding NfL
was similar in both models. MRI reading was performed
on hard copies, which is no longer done in the digital
era. However, at the time of MRI reading for the MEMO
study, the reader followed an established and reliable
protocol.
Conclusions
We found that both NfL and tau serum levels were asso-
ciated with all-cause mortality even when age, sex, and
education were taken into account. However, NfL serum
levels had a better prognostic value and a larger effect
size compared to tau. If comorbidities that were assessed
by a medical interview were additionally taken into ac-
count, the predictive power of NfL serum levels was at-
tenuated. In situations where a medical history is not
available or comorbidities are in subclinical stage, how-
ever, NfL serum levels may provide important informa-
tion for healthcare interventions or the prediction of
mortality.

content.thinking:
Now I have the full paper content. Let me read through the human reviews to understand what they covered, then identify points the reviewers missed.

From reviewing the human reviews, I see the following main themes:
1. MRI methods are outdated, insufficient detail for reproducibility
2. "Atrophy" vs "cortical volume" terminology issue
3. Need for more context on c-statistic changes (0.663 to 0.683)
4. Representative sample concerns
5. External validation of NfL in patient populations (Mielke 2019, de Wolf 2020)
6. Peripheral neuropathy confounding
7. Why do they not evaluate WCML/lacunar infarct differentiation precisely
8. Serum vs plasma sample collection
9. Timing of vascular lesions vs NfL measurement
10. Cause of death discussion (reviewer 3)
11. Lacunar infarct definition inconsistency between tables (reviewer 5)
12. WML quantification methods (Fazekas vs quantitative) - reviewer 4
13. Imputation justification for MRI missing data
14. Multiple comparisons adjustment for regional MRI measures
15. Stepwise regression approach
16. Co-morbidity assessment completeness
17. Added authors need authorship confirmation

Now let me scan the paper for issues reviewers may have missed:

1. Peripheral neuropathy - Multiple reviewers raised this (R2, R5). However, looking at the paper (page 8), they acknowledge this but adjust for comorbidities including diabetes. One concern they may not have fully addressed: They don't have nerve conduction studies to rule out neuropathy for those without diabetes. This is acknowledged as a limitation.

2. MRI slice thickness issue (R4, page 3 of PDF): One reviewer questioned how WML < 3mm could be detected given slice thickness of 5 or 6 mm. Let me look at the methods section... Page 3 states: "proton density (PD)-, T1-, and T2-weighted images acquired with spin echo sequences 

I cannot complete the thought as the next thinking appears to be incomplete. I can't verify the reviewer inquiries using the provided text. The authors don't specify the number or type of coils used, nor do they list technical parameters beyond field strength. Some details around MRI reading protocol remain vague - the reviewer from the Rotterdam southwest group mentions using established reliable protocols but doesn't fully disclose the exact computerized system or evaluation criteria the readers employed.

Additionally, there's a notable inconsistency concerning death certificate categorization. The reviewer points out that death certificates were collected and apparently used for classifying deaths, yet the study doesn't explicitly report how this information was applied. I need to locate the specific reference to death certificates in the methodology to understand whether the categorization occurred or was merely planned for future analysis.

When I review the paper more closely, I notice something about Page 3's Methods section - it does mention that death certificates were obtained and categorized across different cause-of-death categories (all-cause, cancer, cardiovascular, coronary heart disease, and stroke). However, the Results section shows this information wasn't actually utilized to stratify mortality outcomes. Only a post-hoc sensitivity analysis examined stroke mortality.

Page 8 does acknowledge a small dementia death count (n=3), but neither NfL nor tau were tested as predictors for dementia-specific mortality, which limits their prognostic value despite the death certificates being available. The paper also references 27% dementia deaths occurring within that same timeframe, yet this wasn't incorporated into the original predictive models.

I also see a treatment-inference concern on page 5 where the authors specify standardized coefficients per SD increase for NfL and tau, but they don't explain how they'd translate this to individual patient assessment or how to use these coefficients clinically.

Looking at the peripheral neuropathy discussion on page 8, reviewers raised valid concerns about its prevalence in older populations and its potential confounding of NfL levels. The authors note something that needs clarification.

The key issue is that while adjustments were made for comorbidities, there's no information about which participants were screened for peripheral neuropathy or had nerve conduction studies. This creates uncertainty about whether NfL elevations derive from cortical neuron damage or peripheral nerve pathology.

I should verify how the authors handled plasma versus serum samples on pages 2-3 to see if this distinction affects their findings.

On page 2-3, the text clarifies that both serum and plasma aliquots were prepared initially, but due to constraints in previous analyses, only serum was available for this investigation. This sampling choice wasn't fully contextualized in the discussion.

Regarding the lacunar infarct definition discrepancy that Reviewer 5 flagged on Page 4-5, the manuscript tables show 41 participants (15.3%) with included lacunar strokes. The researchers didn't address how they distinguished between the size categories of white matter lesions versus these lacunar infarctions within their methodology.

One unresolved gap involves the publication timing mismatch between the conclusion statement and the statistical results. The conclusion claims both biomarkers independently associate with mortality, yet the subsequent presentation lists only NfL benefits when added to sociodemographic models, not tau. This contradiction warrants clarification in the Discussion.

Given the multi-site reading protocol mentioned for WML categorization, there might be potential inter-rater variability that wasn't assessed or reported. The reference to an established protocol doesn't specify whether reliability metrics were gathered, which lacks transparency for replication.

Examine paper.pdf in this folder. Read the supplied human reviews, inspect the
paper using read_pdf, and do web_search to investigate potential missing points.
Produce your final free-form response about important points the human reviewers
may have missed. Avoid repeating concerns that they already identified.

The following JSON contains the complete human review record for this paper:
<human_reviews>
{"kind": "bmc_peer_review_reports", "parts": {"assets": [{"content_type": "application/pdf", "label": "ReviewerReport_V0_R1", "raw_path": "data_5000/raw/bmc_medicine/2021/10_1186_s12916_021_01915_8/official_review_asset_1.pdf", "status": "collected", "text": "Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 07 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
I reviewed this manuscript that describes the evaluation of demographic, clinical, MRI and
biomarkers in a cohort of individuals recruited from the general population in the 1989/90s and
evaluated in detail in 1997.
The author focused on the group aged > 65y at the time of assessment, and evaluated the inter-
relationship between variables, and the value of baseline variables in predicting mortality.
Overall the manuscript is well written, clear and easy to follow. There are several strengths of the
paper:
- I agree with the authors that there is novelty in their findings
- The long follow up time
- The multi-dimensional data: demographic, clinical (including detailed cognitive), MRI and
biological data
- The correction of regressions for age, sex, years in education
- The high quality figures
However, I have some reservations and comments that I would like the authors to address to try to
strengthen the paper further.
- The MRI methods are unusual, which is almost certainly because the MR data is quite historic,
and was performed in a pre-digital era. However, I felt there was insufficient detail in the paper to
justify/ reproduce the methods. I was unclear how the size-dependent constant was derived and
whether this was subject to any validation. I could not access the Neuroepidemiology reference for
the cortical volume measurements, and suspect others will also be unable. I would therefore
recommend the authors provide more detail on that method and its validity (is it reproducible
between observers, has it ever been validated vs more modern quantitative volume metrics?). I
also found the term "atrophy" misleading as it implies volume change, whereas the authors had a
single scan for each participant. Please consider using a more appropriate description e.g. cortical
volume. Likewise there was reference to "change" at points (e.g. lines 209 and 260), which was
also misleading. I think these points could either be addressed, or they could be better recognised
as limitations.
- Overall the discussion seemed fairly limited and could be expanded. For example, could the
authors help the reader interpret the magnitude of the effect described by a c-statistic change from
0.663 to 0.683. Some further discussion on potential limitations including MRI (above), the
degree to which the research cohort are expected to be representative of the wider "general"
population, the relevance of the associations between tau and mortality in men vs women, the
interpretation of other researchers of sNfL in disease state (a explicit reminder that NfL is non-
specific - of course this is implied by the paper as a whole but I see that conclusion as a key take-
home message from this paper). Finally, why sNfL doesn't increase prognostic accuracy when

brain atrophy or neuropsych scores are included in models: do you feel that serum biomarkers are
more likely to be alternatives to MRI, or complementary to MRI in clinical studies? You touch on
this briefly, but the discussion could be developed a little.
- Minor typographical errors:
*Whilst the English is generally good and the paper is written clearly, there are a couple of places
with grammatical errors e.g. line 85, lines 95-98.
*Abstract says NfL HR of 1.26, but in results, line 244, and Figure 1 it says the risk of death
increased by 27%.

Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 18 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
The authors here analysed serum tau and NfL in a cohort of patients previously enrolled without
pre-defined neurological conditions. They compare tau/NfL levels with neuropsychological tests
and MRI parameters and assess their value as prognostic biomarkers for mortality. The authors
found an association between tau and NfL values and all-cause mortality and between NfL values
and neuropsychological tests score, brain atrophy, and white matter lesions.
Comments:
*Background:
-The authors state that "so far, serum NfL and tau have only been investigated for their prognostic
value in patient population while studies in the general population are missing". Actually, a couple
of studies analysed the prognostic value of NfL in patients without dementia (Mielke et al.
Neurology 2019 and de Wolf et al. Brain 2020), although focusing mainly on cognitive/
neuroimaging outcome. These should be cited and commented on the basis of the authors' data.
*Methods:
-Serum NfL are increased also in patients with peripheral neuropathies, which are quite common
in the elderly (Mariotto et al. J Peripher Nerv Syst 2018 and J Neurol 2020). Did the authors
consider/exclude this comorbidity?
-How did the authors differentiate medium/large WML and lacunar infarction (defined as a
hypodense OR hyperdense T2 lesion of 3-15 mm in diameter)? According to Table 1, none of the
participant had lacunar stroke, which seems unlikely and is not concordant with the association
reported between NfL levels and lacunar stroke (pg. 13 and Table 3).
-Why did the authors collect serum and plasma? Did they use only serum for the analysis or both?
And if they analysed serum or plasma, did they consider the possible difference of NfL values in
the two matrices?
Discussion
-In the last paragraph, the authors discuss the association between vascular changes at the time of
assessment and NfL levels. Actually, we are not able to date the onset of vascular lesions, and NfL
levels seem more reliable in measuring an ongoing/recent axonal damage. This should be
comment and discuss.

elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study

Reviewer's report:
The present study links increased plasma concentrations of NfL and tau to increased risk of death.
The study is well phrased and the statistical analysis seems sound. However, the conclusions
reached seems of modest value both clinically and from a research standpoint. The methods
sections mentions that "death certificates were obtained" and hints that they were used to
categorize the deceased subjects in the study. But, from what I can find, this information is not
used in the study. Why is this? Increased NfL concentrations are known to be linked to
cerebrovascular disease, which in turn characterizes a subject with sever cardiovascular disease
and risk factors. It's not surprising that this would be associated with an increased mortality risk.
The authors need to discuss cause of death in relation to biomarker levels and better highlight the
value of the results reached, or at the very least acknowledge this lack of information as a
weakness of the study. They also need to defend, or better explain, the clinical value of the
conclusions reached.

Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 02 Oct 2020
Reviewer's report:
The study of Rübsamen et al. report on the serum levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL) and tau
protein in a group of 385 elderly patients (>65 yrs.) included in the Memory and Morbidity in
Augsburg Elderly (MEMO) study. The serum levels of NfL and tau were measured using an
highly sensitive technique (single molecule array assays) and were compared with neuropsy-
chological tests and brain MRI result to asses the prognostic accuracy of the biomarkers for overall
mortality in elderly individuals without pre-defined neurological conditions.
1- In section Methods the difference between medium (3-10 mm diameter) or large (>10 mm)
white matter lesions (WML) and lacunar infarcts (defined as "hypodense (T1, PD) or hyperdense
(T2) lesion of a diameter between 3 and 15 mm") is not so clear.
2- No lacunar infarctions are reported in tab 1 while they are present in tab 2.
3- Serum NfL levels are correlated with axonal damage not only of the central nervous system but
also with axonal damage of the peripheral nervous system in acquired neuropathies (Mariotto et al.
2017), therefore the elevation of serum NfL may be due to peripheral neuropathy, whose
frequency progressively increases in the elderly population.
4- In Conclusions the sentence: "We found that both NfL and tau were associated with all-cause
mortality" must be changed because NfL and tau serum levels were associated with all-cause
mortality.
4- The present study demonstrated a predictive value of serum levels of NfL in all-cause mortality,
but does not correlate NfL levels with the different causes of death, in particular with mortality
associated with neurological disease.

Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 14 Oct 2020
Reviewer: Brian Gordon
Reviewer's report:
In the current work the authors retrospectively analyze blood samples take in 1997 as part of the
Memory and Morbidity in Augsburg elderly (MEMO). As part of MEMO participants underwent
neuropsychological testing and a subset had 1.5T MRI scans. They authors are interested in how
blood levels of NfL and tau are related to mortality, neuropsychological performance, and brain
atrophy and white matter lesions. The authors find that primarily NfL is related to mortality,
neuropsychological performance, and changes measured on MRI. The primary strength of the
current work is that it is being performed in a general population study and the length of follow-
up. Prior work has estimated the association of NfL, and even tau now, with MRI measures, but it
is still interesting to see what additional value can be gained by retrospectively adding new
biomarkers to a study. I have a number of points for clarification.
1.Could the authors provide more information about how WML are being quantified? The text
indicates they are being visually read. Is the reader selecting voxels that are abnormal which are
then quantified? My first thought is they were doing a reading like a Fazekas score but this seems
to be semiquantitative. You reference two prior papers from 2000 but a reader is unlikely to go
look those up to read. More information would be very helpful to the reader.
2.Given the slice thickness of your scans, how could you have WML less than 3mm in size? Also
you give the slice thickness, but not the in-plane resolution. This goes back to my first point that it
just was not clear to me how the WML values were being generated.
3.The authors start with a base model that includes age, sex, and education as predictors. They
then assess incremental models adding in additional factors of interest (e.g. NfL). Was there any
structure into how variables were entered into the model? This seems like an example were a
stepwise regression model would be appropriate, but it isn't clear what the authors did.
4.It was clear that you only imputed data when using MRI variables to predict mortality, but why
use imputation at all? What exact variables required imputation and how much of the data was
imputed? Are you imputing variables for all 117 individuals that do not have any MRI data? Did
you have enough data to actually impute any of your MRI variables accurately? Please clarify
what you did and provide justification. I may be more appropriate to simply perform the analyses
that include MRI only in the subset that actually has MRI data.

5.When performing the associations between tau/NfL and neuropsychological tests/MRI did you
include any covariates? Given the strong association NfL has with age, it would be appropriate to
include age a covariate.
6.I originally thought MRI was being summed into one aggregate measure for analyses, but it
looks like you analyzed the associations with individual regional measures as well. Did you adjust
for multiple comparisons?

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 07 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
I reviewed this manuscript that describes the evaluation of demographic, clinical, MRI and
biomarkers in a cohort of individuals recruited from the general population in the 1989/90s and
evaluated in detail in 1997.
The author focused on the group aged > 65y at the time of assessment, and evaluated the inter-
relationship between variables, and the value of baseline variables in predicting mortality.
Overall the manuscript is well written, clear and easy to follow. There are several strengths of the
paper:
- I agree with the authors that there is novelty in their findings
- The long follow up time
- The multi-dimensional data: demographic, clinical (including detailed cognitive), MRI and
biological data
- The correction of regressions for age, sex, years in education
- The high quality figures
However, I have some reservations and comments that I would like the authors to address to try to
strengthen the paper further.
- The MRI methods are unusual, which is almost certainly because the MR data is quite historic,
and was performed in a pre-digital era. However, I felt there was insufficient detail in the paper to
justify/ reproduce the methods. I was unclear how the size-dependent constant was derived and
whether this was subject to any validation. I could not access the Neuroepidemiology reference for
the cortical volume measurements, and suspect others will also be unable. I would therefore
recommend the authors provide more detail on that method and its validity (is it reproducible
between observers, has it ever been validated vs more modern quantitative volume metrics?). I
also found the term "atrophy" misleading as it implies volume change, whereas the authors had a
single scan for each participant. Please consider using a more appropriate description e.g. cortical
volume. Likewise there was reference to "change" at points (e.g. lines 209 and 260), which was
also misleading. I think these points could either be addressed, or they could be better recognised
as limitations.
- Overall the discussion seemed fairly limited and could be expanded. For example, could the
authors help the reader interpret the magnitude of the effect described by a c-statistic change from
0.663 to 0.683. Some further discussion on potential limitations including MRI (above), the
degree to which the research cohort are expected to be representative of the wider "general"
population, the relevance of the associations between tau and mortality in men vs women, the
interpretation of other researchers of sNfL in disease state (a explicit reminder that NfL is non-
specific - of course this is implied by the paper as a whole but I see that conclusion as a key take-
home message from this paper). Finally, why sNfL doesn't increase prognostic accuracy when

brain atrophy or neuropsych scores are included in models: do you feel that serum biomarkers are
more likely to be alternatives to MRI, or complementary to MRI in clinical studies? You touch on
this briefly, but the discussion could be developed a little.
- Minor typographical errors:
*Whilst the English is generally good and the paper is written clearly, there are a couple of places
with grammatical errors e.g. line 85, lines 95-98.
*Abstract says NfL HR of 1.26, but in results, line 244, and Figure 1 it says the risk of death
increased by 27%.

=== ReviewerReport_V0_R2 ===
Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 18 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
The authors here analysed serum tau and NfL in a cohort of patients previously enrolled without
pre-defined neurological conditions. They compare tau/NfL levels with neuropsychological tests
and MRI parameters and assess their value as prognostic biomarkers for mortality. The authors
found an association between tau and NfL values and all-cause mortality and between NfL values
and neuropsychological tests score, brain atrophy, and white matter lesions.
Comments:
*Background:
-The authors state that "so far, serum NfL and tau have only been investigated for their prognostic
value in patient population while studies in the general population are missing". Actually, a couple
of studies analysed the prognostic value of NfL in patients without dementia (Mielke et al.
Neurology 2019 and de Wolf et al. Brain 2020), although focusing mainly on cognitive/
neuroimaging outcome. These should be cited and commented on the basis of the authors' data.
*Methods:
-Serum NfL are increased also in patients with peripheral neuropathies, which are quite common
in the elderly (Mariotto et al. J Peripher Nerv Syst 2018 and J Neurol 2020). Did the authors
consider/exclude this comorbidity?
-How did the authors differentiate medium/large WML and lacunar infarction (defined as a
hypodense OR hyperdense T2 lesion of 3-15 mm in diameter)? According to Table 1, none of the
participant had lacunar stroke, which seems unlikely and is not concordant with the association
reported between NfL levels and lacunar stroke (pg. 13 and Table 3).
-Why did the authors collect serum and plasma? Did they use only serum for the analysis or both?
And if they analysed serum or plasma, did they consider the possible difference of NfL values in
the two matrices?
Discussion
-In the last paragraph, the authors discuss the association between vascular changes at the time of
assessment and NfL levels. Actually, we are not able to date the onset of vascular lesions, and NfL
levels seem more reliable in measuring an ongoing/recent axonal damage. This should be
comment and discuss.

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 24 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
The present study links increased plasma concentrations of NfL and tau to increased risk of death.
The study is well phrased and the statistical analysis seems sound. However, the conclusions
reached seems of modest value both clinically and from a research standpoint. The methods
sections mentions that "death certificates were obtained" and hints that they were used to
categorize the deceased subjects in the study. But, from what I can find, this information is not
used in the study. Why is this? Increased NfL concentrations are known to be linked to
cerebrovascular disease, which in turn characterizes a subject with sever cardiovascular disease
and risk factors. It's not surprising that this would be associated with an increased mortality risk.
The authors need to discuss cause of death in relation to biomarker levels and better highlight the
value of the results reached, or at the very least acknowledge this lack of information as a
weakness of the study. They also need to defend, or better explain, the clinical value of the
conclusions reached.

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 02 Oct 2020
Reviewer's report:
The study of Rübsamen et al. report on the serum levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL) and tau
protein in a group of 385 elderly patients (>65 yrs.) included in the Memory and Morbidity in
Augsburg Elderly (MEMO) study. The serum levels of NfL and tau were measured using an
highly sensitive technique (single molecule array assays) and were compared with neuropsy-
chological tests and brain MRI result to asses the prognostic accuracy of the biomarkers for overall
mortality in elderly individuals without pre-defined neurological conditions.
1- In section Methods the difference between medium (3-10 mm diameter) or large (>10 mm)
white matter lesions (WML) and lacunar infarcts (defined as "hypodense (T1, PD) or hyperdense
(T2) lesion of a diameter between 3 and 15 mm") is not so clear.
2- No lacunar infarctions are reported in tab 1 while they are present in tab 2.
3- Serum NfL levels are correlated with axonal damage not only of the central nervous system but
also with axonal damage of the peripheral nervous system in acquired neuropathies (Mariotto et al.
2017), therefore the elevation of serum NfL may be due to peripheral neuropathy, whose
frequency progressively increases in the elderly population.
4- In Conclusions the sentence: "We found that both NfL and tau were associated with all-cause
mortality" must be changed because NfL and tau serum levels were associated with all-cause
mortality.
4- The present study demonstrated a predictive value of serum levels of NfL in all-cause mortality,
but does not correlate NfL levels with the different causes of death, in particular with mortality
associated with neurological disease.

=== ReviewerReport_V0_R4 ===
Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 14 Oct 2020
Reviewer: Brian Gordon
Reviewer's report:
In the current work the authors retrospectively analyze blood samples take in 1997 as part of the
Memory and Morbidity in Augsburg elderly (MEMO). As part of MEMO participants underwent
neuropsychological testing and a subset had 1.5T MRI scans. They authors are interested in how
blood levels of NfL and tau are related to mortality, neuropsychological performance, and brain
atrophy and white matter lesions. The authors find that primarily NfL is related to mortality,
neuropsychological performance, and changes measured on MRI. The primary strength of the
current work is that it is being performed in a general population study and the length of follow-
up. Prior work has estimated the association of NfL, and even tau now, with MRI measures, but it
is still interesting to see what additional value can be gained by retrospectively adding new
biomarkers to a study. I have a number of points for clarification.
1.Could the authors provide more information about how WML are being quantified? The text
indicates they are being visually read. Is the reader selecting voxels that are abnormal which are
then quantified? My first thought is they were doing a reading like a Fazekas score but this seems
to be semiquantitative. You reference two prior papers from 2000 but a reader is unlikely to go
look those up to read. More information would be very helpful to the reader.
2.Given the slice thickness of your scans, how could you have WML less than 3mm in size? Also
you give the slice thickness, but not the in-plane resolution. This goes back to my first point that it
just was not clear to me how the WML values were being generated.
3.The authors start with a base model that includes age, sex, and education as predictors. They
then assess incremental models adding in additional factors of interest (e.g. NfL). Was there any
structure into how variables were entered into the model? This seems like an example were a
stepwise regression model would be appropriate, but it isn't clear what the authors did.
4.It was clear that you only imputed data when using MRI variables to predict mortality, but why
use imputation at all? What exact variables required imputation and how much of the data was
imputed? Are you imputing variables for all 117 individuals that do not have any MRI data? Did
you have enough data to actually impute any of your MRI variables accurately? Please clarify
what you did and provide justification. I may be more appropriate to simply perform the analyses
that include MRI only in the subset that actually has MRI data.

5.When performing the associations between tau/NfL and neuropsychological tests/MRI did you
include any covariates? Given the strong association NfL has with age, it would be appropriate to
include age a covariate.
6.I originally thought MRI was being summed into one aggregate measure for analyses, but it
looks like you analyzed the associations with individual regional measures as well. Did you adjust
for multiple comparisons?

Abstract
Background: Neurofilament light chain (NfL) is a cytoskeletal protein component whose release into blood is
indicative of neuronal damage. Tau is a microtubule-associated protein in neurons and strongly associated with
overall brain degeneration. NfL and tau levels are associated with mortality in different neurological diseases, but

prognostic markers for overall mortality in elderly individuals without pre-defined neurological conditions. Further,

neuropsychological tests and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain. NfL and tau were measured from non-

biomarkers, concordance statistics based on the predicted 5-year survival probabilities were calculated for different Cox
regression models. Associations between the biomarkers and the neuropsychological test scores or brain structures were

sociodemographic characteristics (concordance statistic 0.684 [0.612–0.755] vs. 0.663 [0.593–0.733]), but not when added

levels were cross-sectionally associated with neuropsychological test scores and brain structures.

Background
Neurofilaments (Nf) are cytoskeletal protein components
whose release into cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and blood is
indicative of neuronal damage [ 1]. Neurofilament light
chain (NfL) CSF levels are increased in several inflam-
matory and primarily degenerative neurological diseases
that result in decreased function of speed and neuronal
loss. Moreover, NfL CSF levels are associated with mor-
tality of patients with parkinsonism [ 2], mitochondrial
disease [ 3], and other neurodegenerative diseases [ 4, 5].
Similarly, this is the case for higher NfL serum levels in
patients with sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease [ 6], after
ischaemic stroke [ 7] and after spontaneous intracerebral
haemorrhage [ 8].
Tau, a microtubule-associated protein in neurons, is
complementary to NfL [ 9] because of its strong associ-
ation with the process of overall brain degeneration. Tau
has also been reported to be associated with mortality in
patients with parkinsonism [ 2], sporadic Creutzfeldt-
Jakob disease [ 6], and intracerebral haemorrhage [ 10]i n
recent years.
The development of single molecule array (SIMOA)
assays [ 11] with increased sensitivity has allowed to de-
fine physiological levels of NfL and tau [ 12] so that sub-
tle increases in the course of subclinical disease can be
quantitated. Based on a strong correlation of biomarker
levels in CSF and blood, this new technology allows to
avoid lumbar puncture and enables high-throughput
analysis of biomarkers in large population-based studies.
In the Rotterdam study, plasma NfL was measured
among 4000 non-demented adults above the age of 55
years [ 13]. A higher plasma NfL level was associated
with a higher risk of all-cause dementia or Alzheimer ’s
disease. Mielke et al. report associations between plasma
NfL and cognitive decline among 79 adults above the
age of 50 years [ 14]. These two studies focus mainly
on neuroimaging and cognitive outcomes, but not on
all-cause mortality.
We investigated whether serum NfL and tau could
serve as prognostic markers (alone or in combination
with other factors) to predict absolute risks of overall
mortality in elderly individuals without pre-defined
neurological condition. Further, we investigated the
cross-sectional associations between NfL, tau, neuro-
psychological functioning, and brain structures.
Methods
Selection and description of participants
The Memory and Morbidity in Augsburg Elderly
(MEMO) is a 1997/1998 re-examination of participants
from the 1989/1990 World Health Organization (WHO)
Monitoring Trends and Determinants in Cardiovascular
Disease (MONICA) Survey Augsburg, Germany [ 15, 16].
Initially in 1989, a random sample of the population of
Augsburg, a city in southern Germany, was drawn from
the office of registration. The sample ’s age range was
25–74 years and the response for the MONICA survey
was 76.8% (4940 participants). For the MEMO study
8 years later, we contacted all participants of the MON-
ICA survey aged 65 years and older on July 1, 1997, and
living in the city of Augsburg or two large, adjacent sub-
urbs. The overall response proportion for the MEMO
study was 60.6% (385 participants). Written informed
consent was obtained from all MEMO participants. The
joint ethics committee of the University of Muenster
and the Westphalian Chamber of Physicians approved
the study.
All participants received a face-to-face medical inter-
view on prior and current diseases and risk factors with
special emphasis on the history of neurological and psy-
chiatric diseases. The diagnostic workup also included a
standardized neurologic examination and the CASCADE
neuropsychological test battery [ 17]. The examination
was done by one of two study physicians specifically
trained for 3 months in an outpatient clinic for movement
disorders. It included parts of the Unified Parkinson ’sD i s -
ease Rating Scale (UPDRS). The neuropsychological test
battery was based on standardized and valid tests assessing
the domains of short-term memory, cognitive speed, at-
tention, and motor speed: Measures of short-term mem-
ory were derived from three word recall tests [ 18]a n d
summarized in a single ‘memory score ’. Cognitive speed
and attention were assessed via the Stroop test [ 19]a n d
the Letter Digit Substitution test [ 20]; they were summa-
rized in a single ‘speed score ’. Motor speed was assessed
via the Purdue Pegboard test [ 21] (referred to as ‘motor

summarized in a global cognitive function score, the
CASCADE score [17].
The diagnoses of diabetes mellitus (type I or II), hyper-
tension, and cardiovascular disease (stroke, transitory is-
chaemic attack (TIA), myocardial infarction, heart failure,
arrhythmia) were self-reported during the interview and
validated by medical records. Blood pressure and body
mass were measured according to the MONICA protocol
and intake of medication during the last 7 days was
documented.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
MRI scanning was performed during the study visit at
baseline on a 1.5-T MR imager (Gyroscan NT, Philips,
Leiden, The Netherlands) at the department of Radiology
and Neuroradiology, Central Hospital of Augsburg, on
average 1.5 h after drawing blood samples. Of the whole
sample (N = 385), 117 individuals did not receive an MRI
due to contraindications (artificial eye lenses or incorpo-
rated metal artefacts including pacemakers ( n =6 9 ) ,c l a u s -
trophobia (n =1 6 ) , d i s s e n t (n =1 1 ) , o r o t h e r r e a s o n s (n =
21)). The MEMO participants with MRI were on average
younger (mean age 72.3 vs. 73.7) than those without MRI.
The MRI protocol included proton density (PD)-, T1-,
and T2-weighted images acquired with spin echo se-
quences with 20 axial slices, 5 or 6 mm thick with an
interslice gap of 1 or 1.2 mm, respectively.
MRI reading for the MEMO study was done at the
CASCADE radiology centre (Department of Radiology,
Daniel Den Hoed Cancer Centre, Rotterdam, The
Netherlands) by a single reader on hard copies using an
established and reliable rating scale [ 22]. White matter
lesions were considered present if these were hyperin-
tense on both PD- and T2-weighted images and not
hypointense on T1-weighted images. The rating scale
assessed subcortical white matter lesions (WML) by
number and three different sizes based on the diameter:
‘small’ if less than 3 mm, ‘medium’ if between 4 and 10
mm, and ‘large’ if greater than 10 mm. Lesions were
counted per size and lobe. An approximate white matter
lesion load was then calculated with the assumption of a
fixed volume per category of lesion size (4.2 μL for small
lesions, 113 μL for medium lesions, and 905 μL for a
large lesion), enabling a quantitative measure for lesion
load. Periventricular white matter lesions were rated
semi-quantitatively per region: adjacent to the frontal
horn (frontal capping), adjacent to the lateral wall of lat-
eral ventricles (bands), and adjacent to the occipital horn
(occipital capping) on a scale of 0 (no white matter le-
sions), 1 (pencil thin periventricular lining), 2 (smooth
halo or thick lining), or 3 (large confluent white matter
lesions). The overall degree of periventricular white mat-
ter lesions was calculated by adding up the scores for
the three separate categories (range 0 –9) [ 22, 23]. Lacu-
nar infarction on MRI was defined as the presence of a
hypointense (T1, PD) or hyperintense (T2) lesion of a
diameter between 3 and 15 mm. Cortical atrophy was
assessed on a semi-quantitative scale with 4 categories
(0–3) rated for each lobe and the Sylvian fissure. These
lobar ratings were subsequently summarized to a total
cortical atrophy score with a range from 0 (no atrophy)
to 15 (maximum atrophy) [ 22]. An atrophy score > 10
(representing the 75th percentile) was defined as the
presence of severe cortical atrophy.
Laboratory measurements
Non-fasting blood samples were collected from each
consenting participant immediately after the interview.
Samples were processed directly in the study centre
within 2 h. After centrifugation, serum and plasma ali-
quots were prepared for long-term storage at − 80 °C.
While the plasma aliquots had been depleted by other
analyses in the previous decades, the serum aliquots had
remained frozen for 22 years. Only serum aliquots were
used in this analysis.
Serum NfL and tau were quantified with commercially
available kits on the single molecule array HD-1 analyser
(Quanterix, Lexington, MA, USA), as previously de-
scribed [ 24, 25]. Samples were run in duplicate by
board-certified technicians blinded to clinical informa-
tion. The coefficients of variation for all samples re-
ported were < 20%.
Mortality assessment
Vital status of all MEMO participants and time of exit
was documented prospectively until December 31, 2015,
on which date the survival times of participants still alive
were censored. The median follow-up time (quantified
with the reverse Kaplan-Meier method [ 26]) was 17.9
years. Death certificates were obtained from local health
departments and categorized in all-cause, cancer, cardio-
vascular, coronary heart disease, and stroke mortality.
None of the participants was lost to follow-up.
Statistical analysis
Age- and sex-dependency of NfL and tau serum levels
were investigated using linear regression with a frac-
tional polynomial for age [ 27]. In all other regression
analyses, NfL and tau measurements were included as
independent variables and were internally standardized
according to the collected data, i.e. any effect estimate
refers to an increase of one standard deviation (SD). In-
formation on comorbidities (any histories of myocardial
infarction, heart failure, vascular surgery, pacemaker,
cancer, diabetes, joint replacement, or trauma with loss
of function based on medical records) was taken into ac-
count in some analyses. Associations between any of the

Cox regression models (adjusted for age, sex, years of edu-
cation, and presence of any comorbidities). Subgroup ana-
lyses by sex were conducted according to Figueiras and
colleagues [28]. Missing values in MRI measurements (co-
variates in the Cox models) were imputed (R package‘mice’
[29] version 3.8.0) with 100 multiple imputations. Under
the missing at random assumption, multiple imputation is
typically more efficient than complete-case analysis (i.e.
smaller standard errors), because it uses also information in
incomplete cases. The imputation model included the event
indicator and the Nelson-Aalen estimator of the cumulative
hazard rate [30, 31], all variables that appear in the Cox re-
gression models plus disease history (blood pressure, dia-
betes, surgeries of the brain, heart, or hip) and general
health behaviour (smoking, alcohol consumption) as auxil-
iary variables. The fraction of incomplete cases among the
observed, which is an estimate for the gain in precision
when comparing multiple imputation to complete-case
analysis [32], was 18% for each MRI variable. To assess the
prognostic prediction performance of the biomarkers, con-
cordance statistics (c statistic) [ 33] based on the predicted
5-year survival probabilities (estimated with 10-fold cross-
validation) were calculated in each imputed dataset. The
point estimate of the pooled c statistic was calculated as the
average of the 100 individual e stimates. The standard error
was computed using both the within and between imput-

calculated for different models: The initial model contained
only terms for age at baseline, sex, and years of education.
Eight further models were constructed by adding either a
neuropsychological test score (memory, speed, motor, or

c statistic refers to the abilit y of a model to distinguish an
individual with the endpoint (dead) from an individual

among two individuals, one dying within 5 years and one
surviving, the individual bound to die will have a higher
predicted risk than the surviving individual will [ 34].
Jack-knife estimation [ 35] was used to assess the c stat-

‘validstats ’ [36] version 1.4). Whenever there was an im-
provement in the c statistic, the respective model was
expanded by adding another predictor, e.g. by adding
NfL to a model containing age, sex, years of education,
and the CASCADE score. This stepwise approach was
done because when statistical procedures are used to
test for incremental prognostic information, the new
biomarker should be tested for significance only after
all other predictors have already been included in the
model [ 37]. In the example above, the test of interest is
whether NfL adds significantly to a model that already
includes age, sex, years of education, and the CASC

before NfL in a stepwise variable-selection process.
In a sensitivity analysis, the initial model contained co-
morbidities in addition to age, sex, and years of educa-
tion. We also repeated these steps using stroke mortality
as outcome to investigate the biomarkers ’ prognostic
value for death due to neurological disease. Stroke was
the only neurological cause of death that had a reason-

Discussion
In this population-based study of elderly individuals
without pre-defined neurological disease, we show that
NfL, but not tau, serum levels can serve as a prognostic
marker for all-cause mortality if no other clinical informa-
tion is available. We also found cross-sectional associations
between NfL and certain domains of neuropsychological
f u n c t i o n i n ga sw e l la sb r a i ns t r u c t u r e s .
Our results show that in population-based settings,
NfL and tau serum levels can be used to identify individ-
uals at higher risk of mortality (reflected by the hazard
ratios above one) that are clinically normal, relative to a
reference group. Our data establish a continuum of pre-
dictive value for NfL between subclinical morbidity and
individuals with neurological disease [ 6–8]. Moreover,
none of the patient- or population-based studies so far
investigated the influence of NfL on absolute risks. Here
we demonstrate that adding NfL to a model based on
sociodemographic characteristics increased its discrim-
inative ability by two percentage points: The probability
that among two individuals, one dying within 5 years
and one surviving, the individual bound to die will have
a higher predicted absolute risk than the surviving indi-
vidual is 66.3% for the model without and 68.3% for the
model with NfL. The latter model yielded a similar c
statistic to the model containing sociodemographic char-
acteristics and the memory score. If a model already

acy for mortality.
If, however, MRI measurements or a full (sub-)clinical
morbidity profile are not available, serum NfL can be
used instead for prognostic models and seems to
harbour important health information in the general
population. This is especially important since serial MRI
measurements are often not available because of contra-
indications or time constraints, are costly, and do not
cover the entire central nervous system.
When focussing on stroke mortality, the incremental
increase of prognostic accuracy when adding NfL was
smaller in relation to neuropsychological test scores.
This was to be expected because NfL is an indicator of
any axonal damage and is, therefore, not disease-specific.
Although neuropsychological tests are easy to adminis-
ter, they are also time-consuming and not applied as
screening procedures to the general population. If con-
firmed and expanded, serum NfL may be the prognostic
marker of choice if blood samples are taken within the
routine check-up of elderly individuals, i.e. serum NfL
may serve as an alternative to MRI in the outpatient
setting.
NfL serum levels were significantly associated with
brain structures involving small vessel vascular disease,
i.e. large white matter lesions and lacunar strokes, at the
time of assessment, but serum tau was not. This is in
line with findings from a study that used NfL and tau
measured in the CSF [ 42]. NfL was also associated with
global brain atrophy while only tau had a small effect
size on subcortical atrophy measures. Serum NfL has
already been reported as a predictor of brain atrophy in
multiple sclerosis [ 43]. We confirm these findings for
healthy individuals.
Strengths and limitations
The long follow-up for vital status with a considerable
high proportion diseased among the study participants is
a strength of our study. Based on the population-based
sampling scheme and the high response rate at baseline,
the MEMO study population is considered highly repre-
sentative for the general German population in the re-
spective age group. The MEMO study was also among
the first ones that used MRI on a population level; there-
fore, we were able to include MRI results into the
analysis.
Among the limitations is the small sample size that re-
duced the statistical power for several analyses. In par-
ticular, it was not possible to investigate the prognostic
value of the biomarkers for predicting death from neuro-
logical disease because only three deaths from dementia
occurred in the MEMO study. Increased NfL serum
levels have also been reported in patients with acquired
peripheral neuropathies [ 44], which are rarely assessed
in population-based cohort studies because of the thor-
ough workup needed, including nerve conduction stud-
ies [ 45]. We were therefore not able to exclude actively
these individuals in our analyses. However, diabetes is
the leading cause of peripheral neuropathy [ 45]. We ad-
justed all regression analyses for ‘any comorbidities ’,
which includes diabetes (i.e. among all individuals with
comorbidities, 40% reported a physician ’s diagnosis of
diabetes). We thereby accounted for the majority of un-
diagnosed peripheral neuropathy cases. We also com-
pared c statistics of models with and without ‘any
comorbidities’ (Fig. 2 and Additional File 1). The abso-
lute increase in prognostic accuracy when adding NfL
was similar in both models. MRI reading was performed
on hard copies, which is no longer done in the digital
era. However, at the time of MRI reading for the MEMO
study, the reader followed an established and reliable
protocol.
Conclusions
We found that both NfL and tau serum levels were asso-
ciated with all-cause mortality even when age, sex, and
education were taken into account. However, NfL serum
levels had a better prognostic value and a larger effect
size compared to tau. If comorbidities that were assessed
by a medical interview were additionally taken into ac-
count, the predictive power of NfL serum levels was at-
tenuated. In situations where a medical history is not
available or comorbidities are in subclinical stage, how-
ever, NfL serum levels may provide important informa-
tion for healthcare interventions or the prediction of
mortality.

From reviewing the human reviews, I see the following main themes:
1. MRI methods are outdated, insufficient detail for reproducibility
2. "Atrophy" vs "cortical volume" terminology issue
3. Need for more context on c-statistic changes (0.663 to 0.683)
4. Representative sample concerns
5. External validation of NfL in patient populations (Mielke 2019, de Wolf 2020)
6. Peripheral neuropathy confounding
7. Why do they not evaluate WCML/lacunar infarct differentiation precisely
8. Serum vs plasma sample collection
9. Timing of vascular lesions vs NfL measurement
10. Cause of death discussion (reviewer 3)
11. Lacunar infarct definition inconsistency between tables (reviewer 5)
12. WML quantification methods (Fazekas vs quantitative) - reviewer 4
13. Imputation justification for MRI missing data
14. Multiple comparisons adjustment for regional MRI measures
15. Stepwise regression approach
16. Co-morbidity assessment completeness
17. Added authors need authorship confirmation

Now let me scan the paper for issues reviewers may have missed:

1. Peripheral neuropathy - Multiple reviewers raised this (R2, R5). However, looking at the paper (page 8), they acknowledge this but adjust for comorbidities including diabetes. One concern they may not have fully addressed: They don't have nerve conduction studies to rule out neuropathy for those without diabetes. This is acknowledged as a limitation.

2. MRI slice thickness issue (R4, page 3 of PDF): One reviewer questioned how WML < 3mm could be detected given slice thickness of 5 or 6 mm. Let me look at the methods section... Page 3 states: "proton density (PD)-, T1-, and T2-weighted images acquired with spin echo sequences 

I cannot complete the thought as the next thinking appears to be incomplete. I can't verify the reviewer inquiries using the provided text. The authors don't specify the number or type of coils used, nor do they list technical parameters beyond field strength. Some details around MRI reading protocol remain vague - the reviewer from the Rotterdam southwest group mentions using established reliable protocols but doesn't fully disclose the exact computerized system or evaluation criteria the readers employed.

Additionally, there's a notable inconsistency concerning death certificate categorization. The reviewer points out that death certificates were collected and apparently used for classifying deaths, yet the study doesn't explicitly report how this information was applied. I need to locate the specific reference to death certificates in the methodology to understand whether the categorization occurred or was merely planned for future analysis.

When I review the paper more closely, I notice something about Page 3's Methods section - it does mention that death certificates were obtained and categorized across different cause-of-death categories (all-cause, cancer, cardiovascular, coronary heart disease, and stroke). However, the Results section shows this information wasn't actually utilized to stratify mortality outcomes. Only a post-hoc sensitivity analysis examined stroke mortality.

Page 8 does acknowledge a small dementia death count (n=3), but neither NfL nor tau were tested as predictors for dementia-specific mortality, which limits their prognostic value despite the death certificates being available. The paper also references 27% dementia deaths occurring within that same timeframe, yet this wasn't incorporated into the original predictive models.

I also see a treatment-inference concern on page 5 where the authors specify standardized coefficients per SD increase for NfL and tau, but they don't explain how they'd translate this to individual patient assessment or how to use these coefficients clinically.

Looking at the peripheral neuropathy discussion on page 8, reviewers raised valid concerns about its prevalence in older populations and its potential confounding of NfL levels. The authors note something that needs clarification.

The key issue is that while adjustments were made for comorbidities, there's no information about which participants were screened for peripheral neuropathy or had nerve conduction studies. This creates uncertainty about whether NfL elevations derive from cortical neuron damage or peripheral nerve pathology.

I should verify how the authors handled plasma versus serum samples on pages 2-3 to see if this distinction affects their findings.

On page 2-3, the text clarifies that both serum and plasma aliquots were prepared initially, but due to constraints in previous analyses, only serum was available for this investigation. This sampling choice wasn't fully contextualized in the discussion.

Regarding the lacunar infarct definition discrepancy that Reviewer 5 flagged on Page 4-5, the manuscript tables show 41 participants (15.3%) with included lacunar strokes. The researchers didn't address how they distinguished between the size categories of white matter lesions versus these lacunar infarctions within their methodology.

One unresolved gap involves the publication timing mismatch between the conclusion statement and the statistical results. The conclusion claims both biomarkers independently associate with mortality, yet the subsequent presentation lists only NfL benefits when added to sociodemographic models, not tau. This contradiction warrants clarification in the Discussion.

Given the multi-site reading protocol mentioned for WML categorization, there might be potential inter-rater variability that wasn't assessed or reported. The reference to an established protocol doesn't specify whether reliability metrics were gathered, which lacks transparency for replication.

Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 07 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
I reviewed this manuscript that describes the evaluation of demographic, clinical, MRI and
biomarkers in a cohort of individuals recruited from the general population in the 1989/90s and
evaluated in detail in 1997.
The author focused on the group aged > 65y at the time of assessment, and evaluated the inter-
relationship between variables, and the value of baseline variables in predicting mortality.
Overall the manuscript is well written, clear and easy to follow. There are several strengths of the
paper:
- I agree with the authors that there is novelty in their findings
- The long follow up time
- The multi-dimensional data: demographic, clinical (including detailed cognitive), MRI and
biological data
- The correction of regressions for age, sex, years in education
- The high quality figures
However, I have some reservations and comments that I would like the authors to address to try to
strengthen the paper further.
- The MRI methods are unusual, which is almost certainly because the MR data is quite historic,
and was performed in a pre-digital era. However, I felt there was insufficient detail in the paper to
justify/ reproduce the methods. I was unclear how the size-dependent constant was derived and
whether this was subject to any validation. I could not access the Neuroepidemiology reference for
the cortical volume measurements, and suspect others will also be unable. I would therefore
recommend the authors provide more detail on that method and its validity (is it reproducible
between observers, has it ever been validated vs more modern quantitative volume metrics?). I
also found the term "atrophy" misleading as it implies volume change, whereas the authors had a
single scan for each participant. Please consider using a more appropriate description e.g. cortical
volume. Likewise there was reference to "change" at points (e.g. lines 209 and 260), which was
also misleading. I think these points could either be addressed, or they could be better recognised
as limitations.
- Overall the discussion seemed fairly limited and could be expanded. For example, could the
authors help the reader interpret the magnitude of the effect described by a c-statistic change from
0.663 to 0.683. Some further discussion on potential limitations including MRI (above), the
degree to which the research cohort are expected to be representative of the wider "general"
population, the relevance of the associations between tau and mortality in men vs women, the
interpretation of other researchers of sNfL in disease state (a explicit reminder that NfL is non-
specific - of course this is implied by the paper as a whole but I see that conclusion as a key take-
home message from this paper). Finally, why sNfL doesn't increase prognostic accuracy when

brain atrophy or neuropsych scores are included in models: do you feel that serum biomarkers are
more likely to be alternatives to MRI, or complementary to MRI in clinical studies? You touch on
this briefly, but the discussion could be developed a little.
- Minor typographical errors:
*Whilst the English is generally good and the paper is written clearly, there are a couple of places
with grammatical errors e.g. line 85, lines 95-98.
*Abstract says NfL HR of 1.26, but in results, line 244, and Figure 1 it says the risk of death
increased by 27%.

Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 18 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
The authors here analysed serum tau and NfL in a cohort of patients previously enrolled without
pre-defined neurological conditions. They compare tau/NfL levels with neuropsychological tests
and MRI parameters and assess their value as prognostic biomarkers for mortality. The authors
found an association between tau and NfL values and all-cause mortality and between NfL values
and neuropsychological tests score, brain atrophy, and white matter lesions.
Comments:
*Background:
-The authors state that "so far, serum NfL and tau have only been investigated for their prognostic
value in patient population while studies in the general population are missing". Actually, a couple
of studies analysed the prognostic value of NfL in patients without dementia (Mielke et al.
Neurology 2019 and de Wolf et al. Brain 2020), although focusing mainly on cognitive/
neuroimaging outcome. These should be cited and commented on the basis of the authors' data.
*Methods:
-Serum NfL are increased also in patients with peripheral neuropathies, which are quite common
in the elderly (Mariotto et al. J Peripher Nerv Syst 2018 and J Neurol 2020). Did the authors
consider/exclude this comorbidity?
-How did the authors differentiate medium/large WML and lacunar infarction (defined as a
hypodense OR hyperdense T2 lesion of 3-15 mm in diameter)? According to Table 1, none of the
participant had lacunar stroke, which seems unlikely and is not concordant with the association
reported between NfL levels and lacunar stroke (pg. 13 and Table 3).
-Why did the authors collect serum and plasma? Did they use only serum for the analysis or both?
And if they analysed serum or plasma, did they consider the possible difference of NfL values in
the two matrices?
Discussion
-In the last paragraph, the authors discuss the association between vascular changes at the time of
assessment and NfL levels. Actually, we are not able to date the onset of vascular lesions, and NfL
levels seem more reliable in measuring an ongoing/recent axonal damage. This should be
comment and discuss.

Reviewer's report:
The present study links increased plasma concentrations of NfL and tau to increased risk of death.
The study is well phrased and the statistical analysis seems sound. However, the conclusions
reached seems of modest value both clinically and from a research standpoint. The methods
sections mentions that "death certificates were obtained" and hints that they were used to
categorize the deceased subjects in the study. But, from what I can find, this information is not
used in the study. Why is this? Increased NfL concentrations are known to be linked to
cerebrovascular disease, which in turn characterizes a subject with sever cardiovascular disease
and risk factors. It's not surprising that this would be associated with an increased mortality risk.
The authors need to discuss cause of death in relation to biomarker levels and better highlight the
value of the results reached, or at the very least acknowledge this lack of information as a
weakness of the study. They also need to defend, or better explain, the clinical value of the
conclusions reached.

Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 02 Oct 2020
Reviewer's report:
The study of Rübsamen et al. report on the serum levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL) and tau
protein in a group of 385 elderly patients (>65 yrs.) included in the Memory and Morbidity in
Augsburg Elderly (MEMO) study. The serum levels of NfL and tau were measured using an
highly sensitive technique (single molecule array assays) and were compared with neuropsy-
chological tests and brain MRI result to asses the prognostic accuracy of the biomarkers for overall
mortality in elderly individuals without pre-defined neurological conditions.
1- In section Methods the difference between medium (3-10 mm diameter) or large (>10 mm)
white matter lesions (WML) and lacunar infarcts (defined as "hypodense (T1, PD) or hyperdense
(T2) lesion of a diameter between 3 and 15 mm") is not so clear.
2- No lacunar infarctions are reported in tab 1 while they are present in tab 2.
3- Serum NfL levels are correlated with axonal damage not only of the central nervous system but
also with axonal damage of the peripheral nervous system in acquired neuropathies (Mariotto et al.
2017), therefore the elevation of serum NfL may be due to peripheral neuropathy, whose
frequency progressively increases in the elderly population.
4- In Conclusions the sentence: "We found that both NfL and tau were associated with all-cause
mortality" must be changed because NfL and tau serum levels were associated with all-cause
mortality.
4- The present study demonstrated a predictive value of serum levels of NfL in all-cause mortality,
but does not correlate NfL levels with the different causes of death, in particular with mortality
associated with neurological disease.

Reviewer's report:
In the current work the authors retrospectively analyze blood samples take in 1997 as part of the
Memory and Morbidity in Augsburg elderly (MEMO). As part of MEMO participants underwent
neuropsychological testing and a subset had 1.5T MRI scans. They authors are interested in how
blood levels of NfL and tau are related to mortality, neuropsychological performance, and brain
atrophy and white matter lesions. The authors find that primarily NfL is related to mortality,
neuropsychological performance, and changes measured on MRI. The primary strength of the
current work is that it is being performed in a general population study and the length of follow-
up. Prior work has estimated the association of NfL, and even tau now, with MRI measures, but it
is still interesting to see what additional value can be gained by retrospectively adding new
biomarkers to a study. I have a number of points for clarification.
1.Could the authors provide more information about how WML are being quantified? The text
indicates they are being visually read. Is the reader selecting voxels that are abnormal which are
then quantified? My first thought is they were doing a reading like a Fazekas score but this seems
to be semiquantitative. You reference two prior papers from 2000 but a reader is unlikely to go
look those up to read. More information would be very helpful to the reader.
2.Given the slice thickness of your scans, how could you have WML less than 3mm in size? Also
you give the slice thickness, but not the in-plane resolution. This goes back to my first point that it
just was not clear to me how the WML values were being generated.
3.The authors start with a base model that includes age, sex, and education as predictors. They
then assess incremental models adding in additional factors of interest (e.g. NfL). Was there any
structure into how variables were entered into the model? This seems like an example were a
stepwise regression model would be appropriate, but it isn't clear what the authors did.
4.It was clear that you only imputed data when using MRI variables to predict mortality, but why
use imputation at all? What exact variables required imputation and how much of the data was
imputed? Are you imputing variables for all 117 individuals that do not have any MRI data? Did
you have enough data to actually impute any of your MRI variables accurately? Please clarify
what you did and provide justification. I may be more appropriate to simply perform the analyses
that include MRI only in the subset that actually has MRI data.

5.When performing the associations between tau/NfL and neuropsychological tests/MRI did you
include any covariates? Given the strong association NfL has with age, it would be appropriate to
include age a covariate.
6.I originally thought MRI was being summed into one aggregate measure for analyses, but it
looks like you analyzed the associations with individual regional measures as well. Did you adjust
for multiple comparisons?

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 07 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
I reviewed this manuscript that describes the evaluation of demographic, clinical, MRI and
biomarkers in a cohort of individuals recruited from the general population in the 1989/90s and
evaluated in detail in 1997.
The author focused on the group aged > 65y at the time of assessment, and evaluated the inter-
relationship between variables, and the value of baseline variables in predicting mortality.
Overall the manuscript is well written, clear and easy to follow. There are several strengths of the
paper:
- I agree with the authors that there is novelty in their findings
- The long follow up time
- The multi-dimensional data: demographic, clinical (including detailed cognitive), MRI and
biological data
- The correction of regressions for age, sex, years in education
- The high quality figures
However, I have some reservations and comments that I would like the authors to address to try to
strengthen the paper further.
- The MRI methods are unusual, which is almost certainly because the MR data is quite historic,
and was performed in a pre-digital era. However, I felt there was insufficient detail in the paper to
justify/ reproduce the methods. I was unclear how the size-dependent constant was derived and
whether this was subject to any validation. I could not access the Neuroepidemiology reference for
the cortical volume measurements, and suspect others will also be unable. I would therefore
recommend the authors provide more detail on that method and its validity (is it reproducible
between observers, has it ever been validated vs more modern quantitative volume metrics?). I
also found the term "atrophy" misleading as it implies volume change, whereas the authors had a
single scan for each participant. Please consider using a more appropriate description e.g. cortical
volume. Likewise there was reference to "change" at points (e.g. lines 209 and 260), which was
also misleading. I think these points could either be addressed, or they could be better recognised
as limitations.
- Overall the discussion seemed fairly limited and could be expanded. For example, could the
authors help the reader interpret the magnitude of the effect described by a c-statistic change from
0.663 to 0.683. Some further discussion on potential limitations including MRI (above), the
degree to which the research cohort are expected to be representative of the wider "general"
population, the relevance of the associations between tau and mortality in men vs women, the
interpretation of other researchers of sNfL in disease state (a explicit reminder that NfL is non-
specific - of course this is implied by the paper as a whole but I see that conclusion as a key take-
home message from this paper). Finally, why sNfL doesn't increase prognostic accuracy when

brain atrophy or neuropsych scores are included in models: do you feel that serum biomarkers are
more likely to be alternatives to MRI, or complementary to MRI in clinical studies? You touch on
this briefly, but the discussion could be developed a little.
- Minor typographical errors:
*Whilst the English is generally good and the paper is written clearly, there are a couple of places
with grammatical errors e.g. line 85, lines 95-98.
*Abstract says NfL HR of 1.26, but in results, line 244, and Figure 1 it says the risk of death
increased by 27%.
